claim: Simultaneous functional MRI (BOLD and ASL) and [18F]FDG PET data were acquired while 22 healthy adult participants performed a cognitive task (Tetris).
source: Simultaneous functional MRI (BOLD and ASL) and [18F]FDG PET data were acquired while 22 healthy adult participants performed a cognitive task (Tetris).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the experimental design and sample size.

claim: The Tetris task had two different levels of difficulty and involved rapid visuo-spatial processing and motor coordination.
source: The task had two different levels of difficulty and involved rapid visuo-spatial processing and motor coordination (see Materials and methods and Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the task characteristics.

claim: Fewer lines were completed in the hard task trials compared to the easy ones (easy 40.5 ± 12.5 vs. hard 32.5 ± 16.7, p = 0.015).
source: As expected, fewer lines were completed (easy 40.5 ± 12.5 vs. hard 32.5 ± 16.7, p = 0.015)
evidence: Statistical comparison of behavioral performance between task conditions.

claim: More games were lost in the hard task trials compared to the easy ones (easy 0.5 ± 1.0 vs. hard 9.8 ± 3.4, p = 10−11).
source: more games lost in the hard task trials compared to the easier ones (easy 0.5 ± 1.0 vs. hard 9.8 ± 3.4, p = 10−11).
evidence: Statistical comparison of behavioral performance between task conditions.

claim: Task performance elicited significant increases in CMRGlu, CBF and BOLD-signals relative to resting-state (all pFWE < 0.05).
source: Relative to resting-state, task performance elicited significant increases in CMRGlu, CBF and BOLD-signals (all pFWE < 0.05, Figure 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis of imaging data showing task-related changes.

claim: Cross-modal changes in CMRGlu, CBF, and BOLD showed high spatial overlap (Dice coefficient = 0.49–0.55).
source: These cross-modal changes showed a high spatial overlap among each other (Figure 2, Dice coefficient = 0.49–0.55).
evidence: Quantitative measure of spatial overlap between imaging modalities.

claim: Significant changes across the three modalities overlapped in the occipital cortex (Occ), the supplementary motor area (SMA), the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) and the frontal eye field (FEF).
source: Significant changes across the three modalities overlapped in the occipital cortex (Occ), the supplementary motor area (SMA), the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) and the frontal eye field (FEF, Figure 2 conjunction map).
evidence: Conjunction analysis identifying common regions across imaging modalities.

claim: Increases in task difficulty (hard vs. easy) caused significant increases in imaging parameters in Occ, SMA, IPS, and FEF (all pBonf-Holm = 10−7 to 0.020), with exceptions for CMRGlu in SMA and CBF in SMA, IPS and FEF.
source: Increases in task difficulty (hard vs. easy) caused a significant increase in the imaging parameters in these brain regions (all pBonf-Holm = 10−7 to 0.020), with the exception of CMRGlu in SMA as well as CBF in SMA, IPS and FEF.
evidence: Statistical comparison of imaging parameters between task difficulty levels.

claim: At rest, significant associations between patterns of CMRGlu and functional connectivity were only observed for the link from IPS to the FEF (pBonf-Holm = 10−7).
source: At rest, significant associations between patterns of CMRGlu and functional connectivity were only observed for the link from IPS to the FEF (pBonf-Holm = 10−7, Figure 3).
evidence: MCM analysis showing metabolic-functional connectivity coupling at rest.

claim: The relationship between CMRGlu and functional connectivity from IPS to FEF was stable across the two task conditions (pBonf-Holm = 10−11 to 10−7).
source: This relationship was stable across the two task conditions (pBonf-Holm = 10−11 to 10−7)
evidence: Statistical comparison of MCM values across conditions.

claim: The functional interplay between IPS and FEF reflects an intrinsic and task-invariant property of brain organization.
source: supporting the notion that the functional interplay between IPS and FEF reflects an intrinsic and task-invariant propriety of brain organization (Fox et al., 2006).
evidence: Interpretation supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Task engagement elicited an interaction effect of condition X connection (p = 0.016) and a main effect of condition for Occ -> IPS, Occ -> FEF and FEF -> IPS (all pBonf-Holm = 0.005 to 0.026).
source: Engagement in the cognitive task showed an interaction effect of condition X connection (p = 0.016) and a main effect of condition for Occ -> IPS, Occ -> FEF and FEF -> IPS (all pBonf-Holm = 0.005 to 0.026).
evidence: Statistical analysis of MCM values across conditions and connections.

claim: Task performance induced increases in the associations between CMRGlu and functional connectivity patterns for Occ -> IPS, Occ -> FEF and FEF -> IPS connections compared to rest (all pBonf-Holm = 0.0004 to 0.02).
source: Post-hoc paired t-tests revealed that task performance induced increases in the associations between CMRGlu and functional connectivity patterns for Occ -> IPS, Occ -> FEF and FEF -> IPS connections as compared to rest (all pBonf-Holm = 0.0004 to 0.02, Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical comparison of MCM values between rest and task conditions.

claim: Task performance was specifically supported by interactions from the occipital cortex to IPS, either directly or indirectly via the FEF.
source: This result highlights that task performance was specifically supported by interactions from the occipital cortex to IPS, either directly or indirectly via the FEF (Figure 3).
evidence: Interpretation of MCM results regarding network interactions.

claim: A putative mediation effect of FEF was suggested by the observation that Occ -> IPS MCM values decreased in the easy condition (from 0.17 to 0.14, pBonf-Holm = 0.017) when controlling for the indirect pathway (Occ -> FEF -> IPS).
source: A putative mediation effect of FEF was suggested by the observation that Occ -> IPS MCM values decreased in the easy condition (from 0.17 to 0.14, pBonf-Holm = 0.017) when controlling for the indirect pathway (Occ -> FEF -> IPS).
evidence: Statistical mediation analysis of MCM values.

claim: Functional connectivity was sensitive to task performance with significant increases from rest to task for all three connections.
source: Notably, functional connectivity was also sensitive to task performance with significant increases from rest to task for all three connections (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of functional connectivity changes.

claim: Bayesian model selection indicated that the most plausible model of neural interactions across both task conditions converged with the one identified by MCM (posterior probability of 0.69 vs. 0.13 for the 2nd best model).
source: Bayesian model selection indicated that the most plausible model of neural interactions across both task conditions (easy and hard) converged with the one identified by MCM (posterior probability of 0.69 vs. 0.13 for the 2nd best model, Figure 4).
evidence: DCM model comparison results.

claim: Family-wise inference showed high probabilities (posterior probability >0.99) for the majority of task-specific modulations (Occ -> FEF, FEF -> IPS) and connections (IPS -> FEF).
source: Results showed high probabilities (posterior probability >0.99) for the majority of task-specific modulations (Occ -> FEF, FEF -> IPS) and connections (IPS -> FEF).
evidence: DCM family inference results.

claim: The Occ -> IPS linkage showed reduced probability for task-based effective connectivity (posterior probability = 0.85).
source: An exception to this was observed for Occ -> IPS linkage (posterior probability = 0.85, Figure 4).
evidence: DCM family inference results.

claim: A contextual modulation of task-specific effective connections as a function of cognitive load was observed for the link FEF -> IPS (p = 0.027).
source: Finally, a contextual modulation of task-specific effective connections as a function of cognitive load was observed for the link FEF -> IPS (p = 0.027).
evidence: Statistical analysis of DCM parameters across task difficulty levels.

claim: Task engagement elicited a marked increase in the association between glucose consumption and functional brain network reorganization.
source: Task engagement elicited a marked increase in the association between glucose consumption and functional brain network reorganization.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding from MCM analysis.

claim: The convergence between metabolic and neural processes was specific to feedforward connections linking the visual and dorsal attention networks.
source: This convergence between metabolic and neural processes was specific to feedforward connections linking the visual and dorsal attention networks, in accordance with task requirements of visuo-spatial reasoning.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding regarding network specificity.

claim: Further increases in cognitive load above initial task engagement did not affect the relationship between metabolism and network reorganization but only modulated existing interactions.
source: Further increases in cognitive load above initial task engagement did not affect the relationship between metabolism and network reorganization but only modulated existing interactions.
evidence: Summary statement of findings regarding cognitive load effects.

claim: Brain function relies on coordinated activity in local neural circuits, from which large-scale functional brain networks are composed.
source: Brain function relies on coordinated activity in local neural circuits, from which large-scale functional brain networks are composed (Park and Friston, 2013).
evidence: Background statement supported by citation.

claim: Changes in the activity of local neural circuits and large-scale systems are paralleled by the modulation of metabolic processes.
source: Such changes in the activity of local neural circuits and large-scale systems are paralleled by the modulation of metabolic processes (Riedl et al., 2016).
evidence: Background statement supported by citation.

claim: Studies have highlighted dynamic brain network reconfigurations when switching from a state of rest to that of cognitive engagement.
source: For example, studies have highlighted dynamic brain network reconfigurations when switching from a state of rest to that of cognitive engagement (Braun et al., 2015).
evidence: Background statement supported by citation.

claim: Solving tasks of increasing cognitive complexity has been linked to complex changes in the functional interplay between cortical regions that otherwise comprise distinct networks at rest.
source: Solving tasks of increasing cognitive complexity has further been linked to complex changes in the functional interplay between cortical regions that otherwise comprise distinct networks at rest (Hearne et al., 2017).
evidence: Background statement supported by citation.

claim: Brain networks exhibit a flexible modular architecture, with highly interconnected hub regions changing their functional network assignment according to task demands.
source: These findings are in line with the proposal that brain networks exhibit a flexible modular architecture, with highly interconnected hub regions changing their functional network assignment according to task demands (Cole et al., 2013).
evidence: Background statement supported by citation.

claim: The BOLD signal represents a non-specific proxy of activation, which is directly mediated by hemodynamic factors including changes in blood flow and oxygen content rather than by neural metabolism.
source: The BOLD signal represents a non-specific proxy of activation, which is directly mediated by hemodynamic factors including changes in blood flow and oxygen content rather than by neural metabolism (Heeger and Ress, 2002).
evidence: Background statement about BOLD signal supported by citation.

claim: The metabolic underpinnings accompanying large-scale functional network reconfigurations that support cognition have received little recent research focus.
source: As a result, the metabolic underpinnings accompanying large-scale functional network reconfigurations that support cognition have received little recent research focus (Horwitz et al., 1995; McIntosh et al., 1994).
evidence: Background statement about research gap supported by citations.

claim: The bulk of functional network reconfigurations occur when participants engage in a cognitive task, with minor reorganizations as a function of cognitive load.
source: Previous work has shown that the bulk of functional network reconfigurations occur when participants engage in a cognitive task, with minor reorganizations as a function of cognitive load (Hearne et al., 2017).
evidence: Background statement supported by citation.

claim: The technique of fPET is sufficiently sensitive to capture metabolic differences between multiple levels of cognitive load.
source: Here we extend upon previous work by providing a comprehensive assessment of the neural and metabolic processes supporting performance in a complex cognitive visuo-motor task. We demonstrated that the technique of fPET is sufficiently sensitive to capture metabolic differences between multiple levels of cognitive load.
evidence: Interpretation of study findings regarding fPET sensitivity.

claim: Regional neural and metabolic changes converge in spatially circumscribed and functionally specialized brain regions.
source: Moreover, our results directly support previous findings, suggesting that regional neural and metabolic changes converge in spatially circumscribed and functionally specialized brain regions (Jamadar et al., 2019; Riedl et al., 2014; Rischka et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation of findings supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The association between glucose metabolism and BOLD-derived functional connectivity strengthened during cognitive performance, compared to a state of rest.
source: We demonstrated that changes in metabolic demands and large-scale network dynamics converge when participants engage in a cognitive task. In other words, the association between glucose metabolism and BOLD-derived functional connectivity strengthened during cognitive performance, compared to a state of rest.
evidence: Summary of main finding from MCM analysis.

claim: The relationship between blood flow and metabolic factors has been demonstrated to be in balance at rest, whereas task-induced neural activations induce a mismatch.
source: The relationship between blood flow and metabolic factors has been demonstrated to be in balance at rest, whereas task-induced neural activations induce a mismatch (Gusnard et al., 2001; Raichle et al., 2001).
evidence: Background statement about neurovascular coupling supported by citations.

claim: CMRGlu and CBF markedly increase compared to oxygen consumption in response to increases in local neural activity.
source: Specifically, CMRGlu and CBF markedly increase compared to oxygen consumption in response to increases in local neural activity.
evidence: Background statement about metabolic responses to neural activity.

claim: The difference between CBF and oxygen consumption is thought to be the major driver of changes in the BOLD signal.
source: The resulting difference between CBF and oxygen consumption is thought to be the major driver of changes in the BOLD signal (Fox and Raichle, 1986; Raichle, 1998).
evidence: Background statement about BOLD signal mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Increases in CBF are linked to glutamate release via both neuronal and astrocytic pathways.
source: Increases in CBF are linked to glutamate release via both neuronal and astrocytic pathways (Attwell et al., 2010; Mishra et al., 2016)
evidence: Background statement about neurovascular coupling mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: The coupling between BOLD changes, local high frequency neurophysiological activity and function implicates the contribution of local recurrent feedback to BOLD, as well as activity reflecting efferent output.
source: The coupling between BOLD changes, local high frequency neurophysiological activity and function (Engell et al., 2012) also implicates the contribution of local recurrent feedback to BOLD, as well as activity reflecting efferent output (Siero et al., 2013).
evidence: Background statement about BOLD signal components supported by citations.

claim: Glutamate release leads to increased glucose uptake into neurons and astrocytes.
source: In fact, glutamate release also leads to an increased glucose uptake into neurons (Lundgaard et al., 2015) and astrocytes (Zimmer et al., 2017)
evidence: Background statement about metabolic responses to glutamate supported by citations.

claim: Glucose uptake provides energy for the reversal of ion gradients and glutamate recycling.
source: to provide energy for the reversal of ion gradients and glutamate recycling (Harris et al., 2012; Magistretti and Allaman, 2015; Raichle and Mintun, 2006).
evidence: Background statement about energy metabolism supported by citations.

claim: The time-dependent, nonlinear interactions between synaptic processing, energy consumption and neurovascular responses across macroscopic brain regions become apparent when engaging in a cognitively demanding task.
source: Although the physiological mechanisms coupling CBF and CMRGlu most likely remain the same, our findings indicate that the time-dependent, nonlinear interactions between synaptic processing, energy consumption and neurovascular responses across macroscopic brain regions become apparent when engaging in a cognitively demanding task.
evidence: Interpretation of study findings regarding neurovascular-metabolic coupling.

claim: The ability of functionally specialized brain regions to dynamically change their connectivity patterns is essential for cognitive processing.
source: The ability of functionally specialized brain regions to dynamically change their connectivity patterns is essential for cognitive processing (Cocchi et al., 2013; Cole et al., 2013; Hearne et al., 2019).
evidence: Background statement supported by citations.

claim: External task engagement is accompanied by the convergence between metabolic factors and functional brain network reconfigurations.
source: Our results extend this knowledge by highlighting that external task engagement is accompanied by the convergence between metabolic factors and functional brain network reconfigurations.
evidence: Summary of main finding.

claim: In a state of rest, the association between glucose metabolism and functional connectivity was confined within the dorsal attention network.
source: In a state of rest, the association between glucose metabolism and functional connectivity was confined within a given functional system, namely the dorsal attention network.
evidence: Summary of MCM findings at rest.

claim: Task performance elicited the emergence of marked interactions between brain regions known to be part of distinct resting-state networks including the visual and dorsal attention systems.
source: In contrast, task performance elicited the emergence of marked interactions between brain regions known to be part of distinct resting-state networks including the visual and dorsal attention systems.
evidence: Summary of MCM findings during task performance.

claim: Task performance elicited the emergence of between-system interactions during visual task execution.
source: These observations support previous results on the emergence of between-system interactions during visual task execution (Riedl et al., 2016).
evidence: Interpretation of findings supported by citation.

claim: Additional cognitive load does not substantially influence the association between metabolic and neural processes.
source: In contrast to the substantial changes associated with the transition from rest to task, we observed that additional cognitive load does not substantially influence the association between metabolic and neural processes (Figure 3).
evidence: Summary of findings regarding cognitive load effects.

claim: Departing from the intrinsic (resting-state) network configuration carries the bulk of the metabolic cost associated with external task engagement.
source: These findings suggest that departing from the intrinsic (resting-state) network configuration carries the bulk of the metabolic cost associated with external task engagement.
evidence: Interpretation of findings regarding metabolic costs.

claim: The functional limits of efficient cognitive performance are largely related to neural processes supporting dynamic interactions between remote brain regions.
source: Considering that the availability of glucose in the brain is carefully maintained (unless experimentally or pathologically altered) (Dienel, 2019), our results put forward the hypothesis that the functional limits of efficient cognitive performance are largely related to neural processes supporting dynamic interactions between remote brain regions.
evidence: Hypothesis based on study findings and cited background knowledge.

claim: Task engagement was associated with the emergence of distinct patterns of effective connectivity from the visual to the dorsal attention networks.
source: Our results showed that task engagement was associated with the emergence of distinct patterns of effective connectivity from the visual to the dorsal attention networks.
evidence: Summary of MCM and DCM findings.

claim: The observed bottom-up processing of visual input is in line with the role of attention networks in stimulus-driven control of attention.
source: The observed bottom-up processing of visual input is in line with the role of attention networks in stimulus-driven control of attention (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Vossel et al., 2014)
evidence: Interpretation of findings supported by citations.

claim: The observed bottom-up processing is consistent with the emergence of feedforward interaction with the FEF following stimulation of the visual cortex via transcranial magnetic stimulation.
source: as well as the observed emergence of feedforward interaction with the FEF following stimulation of the visual cortex via transcranial magnetic stimulation (Castrillon et al., 2020; Cocchi et al., 2016).
evidence: Interpretation of findings supported by citations.

claim: The lack of feedback control of the dorsal attention network over visual areas is consistent with studies showing that top-down modulation only emerges when distractors need to be filtered or context specific information extracted.
source: On the other hand, the lack of feedback control of the dorsal attention network over visual areas is consistent with studies showing that top-down modulation only emerges when distractors need to be filtered or context specific information extracted (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Vossel et al., 2014), which was not the case in our task.
evidence: Interpretation of findings supported by citations.

claim: MCM represents a simplified index of effective connectivity that draws upon the coupling between glutamate-mediated changes in the BOLD signal and metabolic demands.
source: Whereas DCM requires careful a priori selection of regions and specification of a model space, MCM is less vulnerable to these issues (Riedl et al., 2016). MCM represents a simplified index of effective connectivity that draws upon the coupling between glutamate-mediated changes in the BOLD signal and metabolic demands.
evidence: Description of MCM method supported by citation.

claim: DCM provides a formal assessment of interactions between neural populations using a computational model that has been extensively validated.
source: On the other hand, DCM provides a formal assessment of interactions between neural populations using a computational model that has been extensively validated (e.g., Stephan et al., 2008).
evidence: Description of DCM method supported by citation.

claim: The sample size of 22 participants is based on that of the original study introducing the MCM approach which showed robust associations between glucose metabolism and functional connectivity.
source: The sample size is based on that of the original study introducing the MCM approach which showed robust associations between glucose metabolism and functional connectivity (Riedl et al., 2016).
evidence: Justification for sample size based on previous work.

claim: All participants were right-handed.
source: Twenty-two healthy participants were recruited for this study (mean age ± SD = 24.0 ± 3.1 years, 11 female, all right-handed).
evidence: Description of participant characteristics.

claim: The mean age of participants was 24.0 ± 3.1 years.
source: Twenty-two healthy participants were recruited for this study (mean age ± SD = 24.0 ± 3.1 years, 11 female, all right-handed).
evidence: Description of participant characteristics.

claim: Eleven participants were female.
source: Twenty-two healthy participants were recruited for this study (mean age ± SD = 24.0 ± 3.1 years, 11 female, all right-handed).
evidence: Description of participant characteristics.

claim: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee (ethics number: 1479/2015) of the Medical University of Vienna.
source: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee (ethics number: 1479/2015) of the Medical University of Vienna and procedures were carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.

claim: The radiotracer was injected as bolus (510 kBq/kg/frame, 1 min) plus constant infusion (40 kBq/kg/frame, 51 min).
source: The radiotracer was injected via the cubital vein as bolus (510 kBq/kg/frame, 1 min) plus constant infusion (40 kBq/kg/frame, 51 min) using a perfusion pump (Syramed µSP6000, Arcomed, Regensdorf, Switzerland)
evidence: Description of PET acquisition protocol.

claim: The lumped constant used for CMRGlu calculation was 0.89.
source: with LC being the lumped constant = 0.89.
evidence: Description of quantification parameter.

claim: The blood/tissue water partition coefficient (λ) used for CBF calculation was 0.9 g/ml.
source: with ΔM being the difference between label and control images, λ = 0.9 g/ml the blood/tissue water partition coefficient
evidence: Description of quantification parameter.

claim: The longitudinal relaxation rate of blood (R1a) used for CBF calculation was 0.6 s−1.
source: R1a = 0.6 s−1 the longitudinal relaxation rate of blood
evidence: Description of quantification parameter.

claim: The tagging efficiency (α) used for CBF calculation was 0.8.
source: α = 0.8 the tagging efficiency
evidence: Description of quantification parameter.

claim: The duration of the labeling pulse (τ) was 1508 ms.
source: τ = 1508 ms the duration of the labeling pulse.
evidence: Description of acquisition parameter.

claim: The majority of energy is consumed post-synaptically.
source: The main assumption of the approach is that the majority of energy demands arise post-synaptically, that is, in the target region (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Harris et al., 2012; Mergenthaler et al., 2013; Riedl et al., 2016)
evidence: Background statement about energy metabolism supported by citations.

claim: Post-synaptic energy demands are tightly linked to post-synaptic glutamate-mediated processes.
source: which are tightly linked to post-synaptic glutamate-mediated processes (Attwell et al., 2010; Mishra et al., 2016).
evidence: Background statement about metabolic processes supported by citations.

claim: BOLD signal changes receive a substantial drive from post-synaptic activity from distant inputs.
source: Although BOLD signal changes receive a substantial drive from post-synaptic activity from distant inputs (Logothetis et al., 2001)
evidence: Background statement about BOLD signal supported by citation.

claim: The BOLD signal strongly covaries with local high frequency neurophysiological activity.
source: Hence, the BOLD signal strongly covaries with local high frequency neurophysiological activity (Engell et al., 2012)
evidence: Background statement about BOLD signal supported by citation.

claim: Motion scrubbing was applied with framewise displacement threshold > 0.5 mm (plus one frame back and two forward).
source: Here, the framewise displacement was calculated as the sum of frame-to-frame absolute differences across all six motion parameters. Rotation parameters were converted from degrees to millimeters by calculating the displacement on the surface of a sphere (radius = 50 mm). All frames with framewise displacement > 0.5 mm (plus one frame back and two forward) were removed from the further analysis (5 ± 8% of frames across all conditions).
evidence: Description of preprocessing method.

claim: 5 ± 8% of frames were removed across all conditions due to motion scrubbing.
source: All frames with framewise displacement > 0.5 mm (plus one frame back and two forward) were removed from the further analysis (5 ± 8% of frames across all conditions).
evidence: Description of data quality after preprocessing.

claim: Bandpass filtering was applied with cut-off frequencies 0.01 Hz < f < 0.15 Hz.
source: Cut-off frequencies were chosen to enable comparison of functional connectivity at resting-state and during task performance (0.01 Hz < f < 0.15 Hz) (Sun et al., 2004).
evidence: Description of preprocessing method with citation.

claim: The size of the FEF region was 14.4 cm3.
source: The size of these three regions was 14.4 cm3 (FEF), 33.2 cm3 (IPS) and 22.1 cm3 (Occ)
evidence: Description of ROI characteristics.

claim: The size of the IPS region was 33.2 cm3.
source: The size of these three regions was 14.4 cm3 (FEF), 33.2 cm3 (IPS) and 22.1 cm3 (Occ)
evidence: Description of ROI characteristics.

claim: The size of the Occ region was 22.1 cm3.
source: The size of these three regions was 14.4 cm3 (FEF), 33.2 cm3 (IPS) and 22.1 cm3 (Occ)
evidence: Description of ROI characteristics.

claim: The average distance between any voxel of one region to the closest voxel of another region was 46 ± 23 mm.
source: The average distance between any voxel of one region to the closest voxel of another region was 46 ± 23 mm, mitigating potential cross-talk between the regions introduced through spatial smoothing.
evidence: Description of ROI spatial characteristics.

claim: All tested DCM models had extrinsic inputs to the occipital cortex.
source: All tested models had extrinsic inputs to the occipital cortex but differed regarding the absence or presence of intrinsic connections and task modulations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Description of DCM model space.

claim: The reduced probability for task-based effective connectivity from occipital to parietal cortices mirrors the mediation effect of FEF on this connection observed with MCM.
source: The reduced probability for task-based effective connectivity from occipital (Occ) to parietal (IPS) cortices mirrors the mediation effect of FEF on this connection observed with MCM (previous section).
evidence: Interpretation linking DCM and MCM results.

claim: The DCM results did not change when using a larger ROI size of 8 mm.
source: Notably, the DCM results did not change when using a larger ROI size of 8 mm (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Control analysis showing robustness of DCM results.

claim: Calculation of CMRGlu changes independent from the BOLD data showed similar but slightly more liberal task-specific changes in CMRGlu.
source: Calculation of CMRGlu changes independent from the BOLD data showed similar but slightly more liberal task-specific changes in CMRGlu (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Control analysis comparing different baseline definitions.

claim: The overlap between CMRGlu and BOLD-derived changes was comparable between the two baseline approaches (Dice coefficient = 0.53 vs 0.49).
source: The spatial overlap between fPET and BOLD was also similar between the two approaches (Dice coefficient = 0.53 vs 0.49 with the original approach presented in Figure 2).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of spatial overlap between methods.

claim: Spatial correlation of randomly permuted voxels on unsmoothed data yielded MCM values close to zero (z = 0.00005 ± 0.004).
source: As expected, spatial correlation of randomly permuted voxels on unsmoothed data yielded MCM values close to zero (z = 0.00005 ± 0.004).
evidence: Control analysis assessing impact of spatial smoothing.

claim: Smoothing yielded average MCM correlations around zero but with a slightly higher variance (z = −0.001 ± 0.03).
source: Smoothing still yielded average correlations around zero but with a slightly higher variance (z = −0.001 ± 0.03).
evidence: Control analysis assessing impact of spatial smoothing.

claim: Smoothing does not systematically inflate the MCM estimates.
source: This suggests that smoothing does not systematically inflate the MCM estimates, which is also in line with our observation that half of the MCM values were approximately zero despite using smoothed data (Figure 3).
evidence: Interpretation of control analysis results.

claim: Computation of MCM values adopting functional connectivity estimates from an alternative preprocessing approach yielded similar results compared to the original MCM estimates.
source: Computation of MCM values adopting the new estimates of functional connectivity yielded similar results compared to the original MCM estimates.
evidence: Control analysis showing robustness to preprocessing order.
